newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian cabinet approves justice reforms.
newsitem.headline: Italian cabinet approves justice reforms.

text.p: Italy's cabinet on Friday approved proposals for new-style plea bargaining, swifter trials and other reforms in an effort to speed up a justice system creaking under the weight of graft investigations.

A spokesman for Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick said the draft law, which will now go to parliament for debate and a vote, was given the green light at the meeting after only minor changes to Flick's original proposal.

The crux of the package is a plan to allow plea bargaining for all crimes where the maximum sentence is three years, a category which would cover many of the offences committed in the corruption scandals that toppled Italy's old political guard.
Murder, Mafia activities, kidnapping, sexual violence and drug trafficking would all be exempt.

Many commentators have argued that the new-look penal system would provide a way of closing the chapter on the "Tangentopoli" ("Bribesville") scandals which broke in 1992, unleashing a torrent of investigations into corruption in public life.
Flick has denied that his proposals are a way of wrapping up such investigations, saying his aim is to create "a criminal justice system that works better for everyone".
His package has been broadly welcomed by magistrates struggling with Italy's tortuously slow system and by some opposition politicians.
Several hundred Tangentopoli cases have yet to come to court. Legal experts say many could lapse under a statute of limitation unless action is taken to clear the backlog.
Under Flick's proposals, defendants could seek a summary trial under the new plea-bargain system which could spare them jail and years of court cases.
Plea-bargaining has been allowed in Italy only since 1990 and is now limited to a relatively small number of cases.
The proposals would allow judges to impose community service or house arrest instead of jail terms on those who take the new plea-bargain and speedy trial route.
Defendants would also be eligible for up to two-thirds off jail sentences if they paid damages to the state.
